title: Queue
body:
FIFO

enqueue: insert element
dequeue: delete element

#1633-2631 

---

First In First Out. The line at a till: you join the back, you leave the front, and there is
no way to jump. The mirror of the [[Stack]], which touches one end only.

Operations, the same shape as the stack's:

| Operation | Does |
|---|---|
| `enqueue(x)` | insert at the **back** |
| `dequeue(x)` | remove from the **front** |
| `isEmpty()` | nothing to dequeue |
| `isFull()` | array implementation only |
| `front()` | look without removing |

Because the two ends are different, a queue needs **two** markers where a stack needs one:

```c++
class IntQueue {
public:
	IntQueue();
	bool enqueue(int);
	bool dequeue(int&);
	bool isEmpty() const;
private:
	Node* frontP;
	Node* backP;
};
```

`dequeue` on an empty queue and `enqueue` on an empty queue are the two cases to get right:
the first has nothing to return, and the second has to set *both* pointers, because the new
node is simultaneously the front and the back. See [[Singleton List]].

The array version has a subtler problem. Dequeuing moves the front forward, so the space at
the start is wasted and the queue crawls up the [[Array]] until it hits the end with room to
spare. The fix is a **circular queue**: wrap the indices with `%`, see [[Division Algorithm]].
That, or use a [[Linked Structure]] and let the [[Node]]s move.

Queues are everywhere once you know the shape: print jobs, keystroke buffers, the
[[Ready Queue]] a scheduler picks the next process from in [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]], and
breadth-first traversal in [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]], which is also where the cost of each
implementation gets analysed properly.
